claims.text: A refractory high-entropy alloy based primarily on early refractory elements can serve as a low-activation structural material for high-temperature plasma-facing components in fusion reactors.
Vanadium, chromium, titanium, and zirconium are candidate principal elements for the proposed alloy.
The proposed alloy contains its principal elements in a near-equal ratio.
Fusion plasma-facing components experience high temperatures, intense neutron irradiation, and plasma impact.
The proposed alloy has a multiphase, high-entropy microstructure.
The proposed alloy contains nanoscale precipitates.
The multiphase microstructure and nanoscale precipitates contribute to high-temperature mechanical stability.
The multiphase microstructure and nanoscale precipitates contribute to irradiation resistance.
The constituent elements have low neutron-activation potential.
Low neutron-activation potential minimizes the production or persistence of long-lived radioactive isotopes after irradiation.
The refractory microstructure maintains mechanical integrity at high temperatures.
The proposed alloy will provide improved high-temperature mechanical performance compared with conventional plasma-facing materials.
The proposed alloy will provide improved irradiation resistance compared with conventional plasma-facing materials.
The proposed alloy will have reduced induced activation compared with conventional plasma-facing materials.
Reduced activation will lower long-term radioactive-waste issues.
Tungsten-based materials or ferritic/martensitic steels have either higher activation or less favorable high-temperature performance under irradiation than the proposed alloy.
There is insufficient experimental evidence to establish the proposed alloy's exact activation reduction, operating-temperature limit, and irradiation-dose limit in fusion environments.
The composition window that balances refractory performance and low activation remains undetermined.
